Lummi

The Lummi Nation’s 2022 community plan and economic strategy offer community-issued starting points into coastal fishing, education and planning. These selected passages show how the Nation frames continuity and development; they are dated planning accounts, not a current statistical survey or a map of legal boundaries.

Read the sources [2] Lummi Nation [3] Lummi Indian Business Council; prepared by Teresa Taylor, Office of Economic Policy

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Identity and homelands

Lhaq’temish, the Lummi people, are rooted in the northern Puget Sound and neighboring coastal waters.

Read the sources [1] Lummi Indian Business Council

02

Historical context

The Nation describes enduring relationships to fishing, hunting, gathering, and the shores and waters of its homeland.

Read the sources [1] Lummi Indian Business Council

03

Living communities and further study

The Lummi Community Plan explains Sche’lang’en, the Lummi way of life, including language, education, values, ceremonies, and responsibilities across generations.

Read the sources [2] Lummi Nation

04

Reading a community planning account

The 2022 Community Plan introduces the Nation through its institutions and enduring coastal fishing relationships. Its public cultural framing describes a distinctive way of life rather than a list of interchangeable regional customs. This selected reading provides an entry into the Nation’s own planning language; it does not establish current treaty rights or surveyed boundaries.

Read the sources [2] Lummi Nation

05

Fishing, education and development priorities

The 2022 economic strategy connects fishing, trading and sharing with later efforts in education and training. Its introduction discusses the Lummi Indian School of Aquaculture, Lummi Community College and Northwest Indian College as parts of that educational story. Read these as the Nation’s dated account of its priorities, with present programs and outcomes checked separately.

Read the sources [3] Lummi Indian Business Council; prepared by Teresa Taylor, Office of Economic Policy

Lummi Nation Community Plan — selected introduction and public cultural framing (2022) ↗

Read this Nation-issued planning account alongside its economic strategy. Selected introductory paragraphs connect institutions and coastal fishing; the public cultural framing emphasizes a distinctive way of life.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: PDF page 2 (zero-based 1), introductory Nation/institution and land/water paragraphs returned as web lines 3–28. Also read the indexed actual Culture / What We Mean By Culture paragraphs; their page placement was not verified. No claim to a full chapter or the 254-page plan.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Initial public PDF extraction returned actual page text. Later attempts to open culture-page context timed out; no repeated retrieval or bypass followed. The indexed cultural passage was read, but no page number is asserted for it. No maps, photographs, full plan, underlying statutes or current rights/boundaries were inspected. Planning descriptions are not a legal determination or current demographic survey.

https://www.lummi-nsn.gov/userfiles/1034_LummiCommunityPlanFinalDraft20221127-compressed.pdf

Lummi Nation Comprehensive Economic Development Strategy — 2022 introduction ↗

The 2022 introduction connects fishing and sharing with education, training and planning. This is a dated account of the Nation’s development priorities, not current business or population data.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Printed/PDF page 5 (zero-based 4), complete Introduction body under We are the Lhaq’temish, Fostering Success through Education and Training, Strengthening the Regional Economy, and Partnering for Prosperity; web lines 90–119. Cover date/authorship read separately.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Actual public PDF text read. The remaining 84 pages, underlying economic studies, photographs, artwork and current implementation were not reviewed. Historical/2022 institutional statements are attributed; numerical population, acreage, employment rankings, accreditation and present legal claims are not adopted.

https://www.lummi-nsn.gov/userfiles/975_CEDSUpdate042922tnt.pdf
